newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil government clinches crucial reform vote.
newsitem.headline: Brazil government clinches crucial reform vote.

text.p: The Brazilian government pulled off a nail-biting victory in Congress on Wednesday defeating by just two votes an attempt by opposition parties to sink its embattled civil service bill.
Officials announced the government had mustered 309 lower house votes against a left-wing amendment aimed at striking down a central article of the bill.
Government supporters broke into a round of cheers and Michel Temer, the president of the Chamber of Deputies, shouted a loud: "Viva Brazil!" into his microphone.

The article allows the government to fire workers who are deemed incompetent. It also breaks the lifetime job guarantees of civil servants that were enshrined in the constitution but put an increasing strain on the country's public finances.
The government needed 308 votes to kill the amendment, equivalent to three-fifths of the Chamber of Deputies. It had delayed the vote for more than two months, fearing it did not have enough support.
"We are trying to modernise Brazil and this vote was an extraordinary victory for the country," said Political Coordination Minister Luiz Carlos Santos.

President Fernando Henrique Cardoso has insisted that civil service reform, along with a shakeup of Brazil's endebted pension system, are crucial to the long-term prospects of the country's new-found economic stability.

But civil service trade unions have waged a big campaign against the reform bill, bogging it down in Congress for more than two years. Many lawmakers enjoy backing from public sector groups and others have expressed reluctance to back job cuts in the run-up to elections next year.

Cardoso welcomed Wednesday's vote which he said would "allow the state to stimulate its workers to a level of output compatible with the sacrifice of tax-payers." In a statement, the president also said the defeat of the amendment would not put the jobs of hard-working civil servants at risk.

The lower house has yet to vote on a few remaining amendments to the bill before it is put to a second full vote. Once voting on a second round of amendments is completed -- and left-wing parties have said they will again challenge the end to job security -- the legislation moves on to the Senate.
